body: @annevk @domenic @foolip @zcorpan

Why would people have custom bindings for colSpan, of all things? Ugh. Here's Blink's code: https://code.google.com/p/chromium/codesearch#chromium/src/third_party/WebKit/Source/core/html/HTMLTableCellElement.cpp&q=HTMLTableCellElement.cpp&sq=package:chromium&l=57
I feel like ideally browsers would just switch to using reflection. Are browsers opposed to that?

If all browsers agree, and the behavior makes sense (except for being an exception), I'm not enthusiastic about changing it.  But I don't know if browsers are opposed to it.  @bz, what do you think?

(_Do_ all browsers agree?  I'm guessing WebKit/Edge will match Blink/IE, but maybe they aligned with the spec in the meantime, in which case I'm in favor of not changing the spec.)

Here's Gecko's code: http://hg.mozilla.org/mozilla-central/file/29662e28a9c9/dom/html/HTMLTableCellElement.cpp#l386 The comment suggests this was copied from IE and Opera.  This dates back to https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=141818, which clamps colspan to a max of 1000 and also incidentally starts checking for 0.  This doesn't indicate that returning 1 instead of 0 is necessary for web compat.

On the other hand, all browsers seem to clamp colspan/rowspan somehow.  Should we standardize this and have it reflected in the DOM, or should browsers return colSpan/rowSpan as though they're processing the value but then silently not process the value?  If browsers are going to clamp anyway, it seems worthwhile to standardize that and reflect it in the value of colSpan/rowSpan, not require browsers to pretend they're not clamping when really they are.  (We could then also have reftests to test that they're clamping properly for display, not just in the DOM.)
@bzbarsky see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1198#issuecomment-217170120.
In Chrome at least it looks like the clamping that happens in the IDL attribute is not reflected in layout at all. Just based on code inspection, at least.

In Gecko's case there are no custom bindings. What there is, is parsing of the provided string which causes the resulting integer to be clamped. This resulting integer is both used for layout purposes and returned from the getter that wants to return an integer. I just checked this testcase: ```
1 1 700 700
1402
``` and Edge and Firefox agree on it: the cell in the second row is only one column wide. In Blink and WebKit it does seem to be 1402 columns wide.

Previously on HTML: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/757

@bzbarsky what about the zero case? Parsing doesn't clamp 0 to 1, does it?
I guess the real question is: what parsing/clamping are you referring to? Looking at Gecko's code, it doesn't seem to correspond to the spec.

> @bzbarsky what about the zero case? Parsing doesn't clamp 0 to 1, does it? For coslpan? It totally does in Gecko. See the link @ayg provided. I was talking about the gecko behavior here, not the spec. The spec doesn't have any clamping involved. I wrote a testcase for rowspan as well, and it sure looks to me like at least in Blink and Gecko there is layout-affecting clamping going on. The testcase is 3MB, so a bit hard to paste here, and seems to break jsfiddle badly, but it has the following structure: ```
128003
1
64000
64000
Which column am I in and who is to my right or left?
``` If there is no clamping, that fist cell should span across the full height of the table and the last "which column" cell should be in the second column, right? Instead, it's in the first column in all of Safari, Chrome, and Firefox. Seems to be in the second column in Edge. If I change the second repeat count from 63999 to 2000, then it's in the first column in Chrome and Firefox (consistent with clamping in the 65k range), but in the second column in Safari and in the third column in Edge. I have no idea what exactly Edge is doing... in particular, I don't see how that cell can possibly end up in third column, unless I miscounted things somewhere. I also don't know what exactly Safari is doing, short of perhaps clamping to some value more than 66k but less than 128k or so.

This test-case illustrates a display limit of 8190 for colspan in Chrome: ``` html
xxxx
x
xxxx
x
``` The second row of the first table is filled by the cell, and in the second table it stops one cell short, showing that 8191 is treated as 8190. The same test with the numbers changed demonstrates a limit of 1000 in Edge/Gecko: ``` html
xxxx
x
xxxx
x
``` But they treat 1001 as 1, not 1000. 1000 is a much more sensible-looking limit than 8190, but I don't know whether clamping or treating as default makes more sense. All browsers return the value they actually use from .colSpan.

New test: https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/2/

Conclusions for colSpan:
- Chrome clamps to the range [1, 8190].
- Firefox treats values outside [1, 1000] as 1.
- Edge clamps to the range [1, 1000].

rowSpan:
- Chrome clamps to the range [1, 65534].
- Firefox treats values outside [0, 2147483647] as 1, and clamps values between 65534 and 2147483647 to 65534.
- Edge clamps to the range [1, 65535].

I suggest that we standardize Chrome's behavior for both colSpan and rowSpan.  For colSpan, because it's significantly more liberal.  And for rowSpan, because 65534 is the upper bound in two out of three browsers, even though 65535 is more logical.  If Safari matches Chrome here, that's even more reason to spec Chrome.

As far as setting goes, here's another test: https://jsfiddle.net/v21ybof4/
- Chrome treats negative numbers as 0.
- Firefox passes through all numbers indiscriminately.
- Edge throws for numbers less than 1, as well as for some large numbers in the case of rowSpan (not sure which ones).  Where it doesn't throw: for colSpan, it clamps numbers to [1, 1000], and for rowSpan, it passes them through.

I suggest speccing Firefox because it's the simplest.  In all cases, layout needs to match the returned value from the DOM property.

(The current spec does assign meaning to rowspan=0, so we have to allow that as well for now.  But Chrome/Edge don't implement it, although Firefox does, so I don't know if we want to bother keeping that feature.)
Submitted PR #1993.

> Chrome clamps to the range [1, 8190].
> Chrome clamps to the range [1, 65534].

Those are not what Chrome does, as you can tell by looking at https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/5/.  I may be willing to implement what Chrome does here, modulo the discussion below, but certainly not what you're trying to have the spec say in your pull request.

> For colSpan, because it's significantly more liberal.

The reason Gecko is not more liberal here is that we encountered miscoded pages with severe performance and memory issues due to large colspans.  I doubt we would be willing to increase our colspan cap here.  But see below.

> If Safari matches Chrome here, that's even more reason to spec Chrome.

Safari doesn't match Chrome, and I'm not sure why you didn't bother testing Safari yourself, or at least asking someone for data on it, before changing specs around.  Again testing on https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/5/ the Safari behavior for both colspan and rowspan is that values outside [0, 2147483647]  are treated as "1" and values inside that range are left as-is, no clamping.

What's not clear from any of these testcases is what the colspan/rowspan values used for _layout_ are in any of these browsers.  Does Safari really create a table with 2 billion columns if you do colspan="2000000000"?  Or is it just having the colspan getter report a number that's totally unrelated to the actual layout behavior?  I strongly suggest you at least get this part cleared up with the WebKit folks, again before you start changing the spec.  If we don't care about the getter matching layout, then Gecko could obviously claim 8190 in the getter and cap to 1000 in layout, which would solve the performance issues I mention above, at the cost of having the getter lie.  But your last sentence suggests you do care about having the getter match layout...

> As far as setting goes, here's another test: https://jsfiddle.net/v21ybof4/
> Chrome treats negative numbers as 0.

Yes, as far as I can tell, which is ... quite odd.  I don't understand how their behavior on https://jsfiddle.net/v21ybof4/3/ can be reconciled with this being an "unsigned long" IDL attribute (which it is in their IDL).

Safari's behavior is pretty simple: they do normal "unsigned long" IDL processing, then any number outside the range [0, 2147483647] is converted to 1.

> Firefox passes through all numbers indiscriminately.

Not quite, as you can see from the testcase at https://jsfiddle.net/v21ybof4/3/.

What Firefox does is normal IDL "unsigned long" processing, then takes the resulting 32-bit unsigned int, reinterprets the bits as a signed 32-bit int in 2s complement notation, converts that to a string, and passes it to setAttribute.  This is completely insane and we should not spec this behavior; I'm 99% we have existing Gecko bugs on that "reinterpret as signed int" crap.  Luckily, your proposed spec text does not match Firefox here.  Of course it doesn't match anyone else either...

@bzbarsky Thank you for your feedback, which is essential and enlightening as always.  :)

> Those are not what Chrome does, as you can tell by looking at https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/5/. I may be willing to implement what Chrome does here, modulo the discussion below, but certainly not what you're trying to have the spec say in your pull request.

Looking at https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/5/ in Chrome, I see that it behaves as I described, AFAICT, except that values larger than 4294967295 are clamped to 1 instead of the max value (maybe because of wrapping).  What difference are you observing?  I get the following:

```
        -5  -1  0   1000    1001    8190    8191    65534   65535   2147483647  2147483648  2147483652  4294967295  4294967296  5000000000
colspan 1   1   1   1000    1001    8190    8190    8190    8190    8190        8190        8190        8190        1           1
rowspan 1   1   1   1000    1001    8190    8191    65534   65534   65534       65534       65534       65534       1           1
```

I don't feel the need to spec the behavior for values above 2^32, but if you really want, we could.

> The reason Gecko is not more liberal here is that we encountered miscoded pages with severe performance and memory issues due to large colspans. I doubt we would be willing to increase our colspan cap here. But see below.

Even just from 1000 to 8190?  Hopefully Chrome would be okay with a smaller cap -- @domenic, do you think you could lower it to 1000 to match Firefox/Edge if Firefox doesn't want to increase it?

> Safari doesn't match Chrome, and I'm not sure why you didn't bother testing Safari yourself, or at least asking someone for data on it, before changing specs around. Again testing on https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/5/ the Safari behavior for both colspan and rowspan is that values outside [0, 2147483647] are treated as "1" and values inside that range are left as-is, no clamping.

This doesn't sound reasonable, because it almost certainly doesn't match layout, so I'm happy to ignore it.  I don't test WebKit because I have no access to any OS X machine, and nobody has been able to tell me a way to test it on Windows or Linux.  Sometimes I ask people to test for me, and you're right that I should do so before making PRs (if I can find them).

> What's not clear from any of these testcases is what the colspan/rowspan values used for layout are in any of these browsers.

In w3c/web-platform-tests#4115, I include [a test](http://w3c-test.org/submissions/4115/html/semantics/tabular-data/processing-model-1/span-limits.html) for layout (using getBoundingClientRect()).  Please test in WebKit and report back!

> Luckily, your proposed spec text does not match Firefox here. Of course it doesn't match anyone else either...

When browsers disagree so widely, the spec probably isn't going to match any of them exactly.  But that's probably okay, because if they could get away with so much disagreement without bugs filed against them, it suggests it doesn't matter much for web compat.  (Unless there's browser-sniffing going on, but in this case, I somehow don't think many sites are browser-sniffing to decide how best to set a colspan of 5000000000.)

In Safari (including its Technology Preview) for [this test](http://w3c-test.org/submissions/4115/html/semantics/tabular-data/processing-model-1/span-limits.html) I get:
- pass
- assert_equals: expected 22.109375 but got 35.21875
- assert_equals: expected 393335 but got 49271
- assert_equals: expected 393335 but got 49271

> except that values larger than 4294967295 are clamped to 1 instead of the max value

Precisely.

> maybe because of wrapping

Hard to say.  See https://jsfiddle.net/drjpzce9/6/

Luckily, you don't have to guess: you can just look at the relevant code.  It looks like this:

```
unsigned value = 0;
if (colSpanValue.isEmpty() || !parseHTMLNonNegativeInteger(colSpanValue, value))
    return 1;
return max(1u, min(value, maxColSpan));
```

where `maxColSpan` is 8192.  If you dig through `parseHTMLNonNegativeInteger` it validates the string (makes sure it's only sign and digits, etc) and then calls `charactersToUIntStrict`, which will fail out if the number it's trying to create doesn't fit inside an `unsigned` on the platform involved.  In particular, Chrome's behavior is different on platforms with 16-bit `unsigned`, 32-bit `unsigned`, and 64-bit `unsigned`.

Now that we have that sorted out, we probably shouldn't spec Chrome's behavior exactly as-is, of course.  ;)  My main concerns for the behavior are:
1. That we do not force implementations to do bigint anything.
2. That the behavior we define is well-defined independent of the size of `unsigned` and whatnot.

A secondary concern may be that we not introduce the complexity of telling apart "not a number" and "overflowed" by giving them different behavior.  In Gecko in particular this doesn't introduce a huge burden, I guess; we already communicate that information to the caller, but in Chrome's case distinguishing those cases would take some restructuring of all this code.  I can't speak to other implementors.

I guess also given all that I take back "I wouldn't want to implement what's in the spec", since I can just treat overflow as whatever max value is decided on.  But please do talk to other implementors here before making spec changes.

> I don't feel the need to spec the behavior for values above 2^32

Why exactly not?  What's the point of having a spec that doesn't spec things?

> Even just from 1000 to 8190?

The correct phrasing of that question is: "even from just 1GB of RAM to 8GB or RAM?"

Yes, even just that.

> This doesn't sound reasonable, because it almost certainly doesn't match layout

You should really test/check this instead of just guessing.  Talk to the Safari folks.  @cdumez replies to things, for example, and can probably forward along questions if he doesn't know the answer offhand himself.

> I don't test WebKit because I have no access to any OS X machine

Do you have access to browserstack?  If not, it's really not that hard to ask people to test things on Mac for you (e.g. I can do it), or to just go read WebKit's code in the worst case; it _is_ open-source... Again, asking may be simpler than sorting through the code, esp. where layout is involved.

> In w3c/web-platform-tests#4115, I include a test for layout (using getBoundingClientRect()). 

I get the same results as @annevk here.

> When browsers disagree so widely, the spec probably isn't going to match any of them exactly

Sure.  I just want us to be clear on whether we are or are not matching behaviors of browsers, which behaviors we are or are not matching, and whether we've made a conscious decision to not match or just forgot to test some cases.  And if we're not actually matching behavior, to not claim we are in PRs, or at least clearly describe where we're matching it and where we're not.  ;)

> Why exactly not? What's the point of having a spec that doesn't spec things? I meant, I don't see the need to spec _Chrome's_ behavior for values above 2^32. I think they should be clamped instead of resetting to 1, even though Chrome doesn't. I did notice my proposed spec's deviation from Chrome's behavior, and thought I mentioned somewhere that it was deliberate, but maybe I didn't. > But please do talk to other implementors here before making spec changes. That's what comments on PRs (or issues) are for! I didn't make any spec changes, and can't, because I don't have write access to this repo. > The correct phrasing of that question is: "even from just 1GB of RAM to 8GB or RAM?" > > Yes, even just that. I don't have any problem with speccing 1000, particularly because Edge also does it, provided Chrome and WebKit are willing to converge. > Do you have access to browserstack? Good suggestion. I'm working on it. For now, I used Safari 7.1 on their free edition, and found that their limit for colspan is 536870910 (?!): ``` html
aa
a
aa
a
``` And I wrote a script to figure out rowspan at https://jsfiddle.net/yuhyf0g6/6/, which identified that Safari 7.1's maximum rowspan seems to be 8190. Here's a fiddle to illustrate it (change "val" to 8190): https://jsfiddle.net/ncm42axp/1/ And here's one to automatically identify colspan, while I'm at it, although it seems to give very strange results in Edge: https://jsfiddle.net/vwhj9ph6/2/ If anyone could test with the JSFiddles from the previous paragraph to figure out if this is still true in latest Safari (while I work on maybe getting it on BrowserStack), please do! > Sure. I just want us to be clear on whether we are or are not matching behaviors of browsers, which behaviors we are or are not matching, and whether we've made a conscious decision to not match or just forgot to test some cases. And if we're not actually matching behavior, to not claim we are in PRs, or at least clearly describe where we're matching it and where we're not. ;) Okay, okay. I'm still happy with the PR's actual content, except maybe reducing the cap on colspan to 1000 if Firefox/Edge can't do it. @cdumez, do you think WebKit would be okay on capping colspan in line with other browsers, to either 1000 or 8190?

/cc @foolip @tkent-google to see if Chrome would be interested in changing its colspan-capping behavior per something like https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/1993. From what I understand of the above exchange, the PR description is not entirely accurate, as Chrome's behavior depends on whether it's running on a 32- or 64-bit platform. And we're also contemplating changing the limit from 8190 to 1000 since that's what Gecko does.

Chrome's behavior will vary based on platform only for values on the order of 2^32, so I don't think it will pose any compatibility issues.  Note that the PR also specifies behavior for _setting_ colspan/rowspan that's different from Chrome.

> as Chrome's behavior depends on whether it's running on a 32- or 64-bit platform

Not quite.  Most 64-bit platforms still have `int` as a 32-bit type.  So in practice, Chrome's behavior may be identical across all platforms it actually supports.

> I don't see the need to spec Chrome's behavior for values above 2^32

OK, that makes sense.

> I think they should be clamped instead of resetting to 1

OK.  As I said above, I can live with that, because Gecko already distinguishes between "invalid character in value" and "overflow".  But please check with other implementors whether they're willing to do that.  Explicit ccs are more or less needed for that sort of thing; most people are sane and do not watch this entire repo.  ;)

> And I wrote a script to figure out rowspan at https://jsfiddle.net/yuhyf0g6/6/

This outputs 8190 for me in both a WebKit nightly and Safari 10.  Note that I did not review the script; I can do that if you want.

> And here's one to automatically identify colspan, while I'm at it, although it seems to give very strange results in Edge: https://jsfiddle.net/vwhj9ph6/2/

WebKit nightly and Safari both give me 33554430 for this one.  That's a rather odd number; I have no idea where it's coming from!

@domenic @foolip @tkent-google In addition to whether you're okay with reducing your colspan limit from 8190 to 1000 to match Gecko and Edge (Boris doesn't want to raise the limit in Gecko because of OOM), can you clamp numbers above 2^32 to 1000 (or 65534 for rowspan) instead of resetting them to 1?  Or can you not distinguish between overflow and other invalid values here?

@cdumez Can WebKit make the following changes?  1) Impose colspan limit of 1000 (currently seems to be much higher).  2) Increase rowspan limit from 8190 to 65534.  3) Clamp arbitrarily large values to 1000 or 65534 instead of setting to 1 (this requires being able to distinguish between "too large" and "invalid number").  (Possibly you already do this, my test didn't seem to work.)
I guess, if it leads to interoperability. We can try and align.
Do we have any evidence that colspan>1000 is not used in the web?

No.  In fact we have evidence that ridiculous colspans (for various values of "ridiculous") _are_ used, typically by mistake.  That's why browsers all have some sort of cap on how big a colspan they will actually support.
@tkent-google any further thoughts on aligning with @ayg's proposal?

> @tkent-google any further thoughts on aligning with @ayg's proposal?

It's ok for returning 1 for colspan=0.  I confirmed Blink/Edge/WebKit didn't have rowspan=0 behavior, and want to remove it from the specification.
